title: One outer product updates many output values
text: One outer product updates many output values
Matrix multiplication is a sum of outer products: C += A[:, k] × B[k, :].
Sources: Arm ACLE [1] · Hello SME microbenchmarks [2] · numerical example constructed for this deck
On this M4 Pro: 16 FP32 lanes × 16 lanes = 256 output updates per FMOPA.
256 fused multiply-adds = 512 nominal FLOPs per FP32 FMOPA.

title: ZA holds four logical FP32 tiles on this M4 Pro
text: ZA holds four logical FP32 tiles on this M4 Pro
Scalable means the register dimensions depend on the streaming vector length (SVL).
Sources: Arm ACLE [1] · Hello SME [2] · src/runtime.c · examples/m4-pro/environment.json
A Z vector: 512 bits = 16 FP32 values

SVL / 32 = 16 lanes
ZA storage = 64 × 64 bytes
4 × (16 × 16 × 4) = 4096 bytes

The ISA can scale; this kernel is deliberately
specialized for 512-bit SVL.
Four independent tile accumulators let the kernel interleave its updates.

title: Transpose A inside ZA to build contiguous panels
text: Transpose A inside ZA to build contiguous panels
Load horizontal slices, read vertical groups, then store packed columns.
Source: src/sme_pack.c · src/pack.c · intrinsic semantics: Arm ACLE [1]
Actual block: 16 horizontal loads → 4 vertical-group reads → 4 grouped stores.
For every k, A[k*16 + lane] now supplies 16 consecutive output-row values.

title: For small matrices, avoid packing B entirely
text: For small matrices, avoid packing B entirely
At N≤512, adjacent B columns are already contiguous in the original row-major input.
Source: src/sme_opt.c: direct_b · src/pack_opt.c: pack_inputs_opt · saved paired speedups

A → pack A16
B → pack B16 → compute

A → transpose in ZA
B → direct row-major loads → compute
The small-size gain comes mostly from preparing less data, more efficiently.

title: Reshape the large-matrix kernel to 16×64
text: One A vector feeds four FMOPA instructions; B arrives as a four-vector group.
Source: src/sme_opt.c: tile_16x64 · src/pack_opt.c · FP32/SVL=512 arithmetic
Both shapes: 2048 FLOPs/k. Operand loads: 256 B/k (32×32) vs 320 B/k (16×64).
The gain comes from the complete load/layout/blocking design, not fewer operand bytes.

title: Keep the loaded tuple local to each K iteration
text: Keep the loaded tuple local to each K iteration
Generated instructions matter: inspect the compiler output as well as the C source.
Source: src/sme_opt.c: tile_16x64 comment and loop · build.py · build/sme_opt.disasm.txt

Load tuple
Consume four B vectors
End tuple lifetime
Repeat, unrolled ×4
Tuning observation: a tuple carried across iterations generated 5 extra SSVE copies/k.
Keep live ranges short and check the actual disassembly on the compiler you use.

title: Use larger K blocks and bounded M/N traversal
text: Use larger K blocks and bounded M/N traversal
Final compute blocks: KC=2048, MC=256, NC=512. Microkernel: 16×64.

MC × KC
256 × 2048 FP32

16-row micro-panels

KC × NC
2048 × 512 FP32

Original: 16 K passes
Optimized: 2 K passes
Fewer partial-C updates
Reload only after pass 1
Loop order: K block → N block → M block → 64 columns → 16 rows.
Larger K blocks reduce partial-C traffic; M/N blocks organize operand reuse.

title: Tile B packing so source and destination stay local
text: Tile B packing so source and destination stay local
Large B is copied in 32-row × 256-column chunks, then stored as K×64 panels.

A chunk = 32 K rows × 256 columns
32 KiB of logical FP32 source values

Compute loads 64 consecutive floats
per k using one vector-group load.
Do not trade a faster compute loop for expensive scattered writes in the packer.
